extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of moral philosophy; scholars evaluating Kantian ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria for assessing Kant's moral philosophy (Categorical Imperative, dignity, conscience, freedom/necessity) as presented and criticized in the chapter. Useful for scholars or students judging the conceptual, empirical, and practical adequacy of ethical theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thinkability / conceptual coherence of foundational concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundational ethical concepts must be thinkable and not self-contradictory; Kant's definition of 'dignity' as 'an unconditioned, incomparable value' is criticized as a 'hollow hyperbole' and a 'contradictio in adjecto.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every value is comparative (an estimation of one thing compared with another); asserting an 'incomparable, unconditioned, absolute value' is like asserting the 'highest number'—a concept that cannot be coherently conceived. Check for hidden contradictions when adjectives render a concept unthinkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical grounding / justificatory credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about moral realities must have justificatory credentials; if something cannot be conceived as possible or proved actual, the claimant bears the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Categorical Imperative is 'expressly not put forward as a fact of consciousness, nor otherwise founded on experience,' and Kant warns against explaining it by empirical anthropology. A robust ethical theory should either be empirically grounded or provide adequate non-empirical justification; absence of both invites scepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical efficacy / provision of motive
rubrics_metrics.description: A moral principle should plausibly provide motive and interest for action; the text questions 'how Pure Reason ... can by itself be practical' and supply motive without antecedent object for the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a purportedly practical principle cannot account for why agents would be motivated to act (i.e., how it produces interest or motive), its practical relevance is doubtful. Evaluate whether abstract principles can plausibly generate moral motivation in ordinary consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological plausibility regarding conscience (temporal relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience, unlike a categorical imperative, speaks after an act rather than before; it draws its material from experience—'Conscience is thus the knowledge that a man has about what he has done.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a moral theory properly accounts for the temporal and empirical character of conscience: conscience as retrospective, experience-based self-knowledge, not an a priori legislative voice that necessarily issues prescriptive commands prior to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of metaphor and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of legal/judicial terminology to describe inner moral life (indictment, judge, plaintiff, sentence) may be misleading; such metaphors are not inherently suited to capture the 'most secret stirrings of the human heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether rhetorical/legal metaphors over-dramatize or distort psychological phenomena; distinguish between useful analogies and metaphorical dressings that create unjustified impressions of objectivity or authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of theological smuggling / hidden assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A purportedly secular ethics should not covertly rest on theological assumptions; the text argues Kant's system masks theological Ethics (e.g., doctrine of the Highest Good, Postulates of Practical Reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe ethical systems for tacit theological postulates or circular inferences where alleged a priori foundations actually presuppose the very theological commitments they claim to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of personification/supernatural assumptions about conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not attribute to conscience a personified, omniscient judge or superhuman executive authority; such constructs lead from conscience to superstition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the theory unjustifiably posits supernatural or omniscient inner agencies to avoid apparent contradictions (e.g., making the judge 'another person'). Prefer accounts that explain moral self-reproach without invoking supernatural personifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between a priori claims and empirical absence of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: If an imperative is claimed to be of such a kind that 'no instance can show, and consequently there can be no empirical proof, that an Imperative of this sort exists everywhere,' then asserting its reality without empirical instances is suspicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the coherence of claiming universal moral imperatives while conceding that no empirical instance can demonstrate them; ask whether such claims rest on convincing non-empirical argumentation or are merely rhetorical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power on freedom vs necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory theory should account for the coexistence of freedom and necessity; Kant's distinction of intelligible vs empirical character is praised for resolving apparent contradiction between moral responsibility and causal determinism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge theories by their ability to explain how moral responsibility and the felt sense of freedom can coexist with causal necessity in action—e.g., whether locating freedom in 'esse' (being) rather than 'operari' (doing) is a coherent and illuminating move.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper locus of moral responsibility (being vs doing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral responsibility ultimately touches 'what one is' (esse) rather than merely 'what one does' (operari); conscience accuses the 'esse' while deeds furnish incriminating evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an ethical theory correctly locates responsibility and accounts for why agents feel culpable in virtue of character, not merely individual acts; consider whether this account matches ordinary moral practices and intuitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of pedantry that produces fatalism or absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical systems should not, by excessive abstraction or pedantry, devolve into a form of moral fatalism or comic absurdity (as charged of Fichte's magnification of Kant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether normative formulations, when carried to consequences, imply rigid deterministic moral fates or absurd prescriptions that disconnect from actual human behaviour and moral practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical basis of conscience as knowledge of past deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience is 'knowledge that a man has about what he has done'—it is empirical, certain (gewiss), and distinct from problematic thoughts; deeds, not mere inclinations, burden conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral psychology within a theory, verify that the account respects the empirical character of conscience (retrospective, evidence-based) and does not attribute responsibility to mere transient thoughts or impulses without action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-uniqueness of judicial form in self-reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial form (indictment, defence, judge) is not peculiar to moral conscience but commonly applies to many forms of self-reflection (e.g., financial regret, social embarrassment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about treating a particular metaphorical form as uniquely diagnostic of moral phenomena; distinguish features that are genuinely ethical from general modes of reflective self-evaluation.
